fields.title: Yakor: Goals Met, Business Down
fields.summary: All teams hit their goals, but the business failed to grow. Decide how to set goals going forward.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you propose for next year?
fields.brief/role: You are a product manager at Yakor, responsible for product goal setting.
fields.brief/company: Yakor is a fictional booking service for meeting rooms and workspaces for companies: 800 corporate clients.
fields.brief/context: The year has ended: seven out of nine team goals were achieved, and everyone is celebrating. However, revenue grew by 4% instead of the planned 25%, client churn increased, and no one can explain the discrepancy in meetings.
fields.brief/objective: Figure out what happened with the goals and propose how to set them for next year.
fields.brief/constraints: Three weeks until planning. Five product teams.
fields.brief/task: Choose an approach and justify it.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Goals achieved and results delivered are different things
fields.learnTakeaway/body: A goal framed as work gets completed by releasing a feature—and changes nothing. A goal framed as a metric tied to a bonus gets gamed. What works is a combination: one top-level metric, driver metrics underneath it within team influence, and guardrail metrics alongside. And check goals by breakdowns: growth that comes entirely from already active clients is usually not the growth you were aiming for.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
Nine goals across five teams. Formulations:

"Launch mobile app" — achieved.
"Build calendar integration" — achieved.
"Increase number of bookings by 30%" — achieved (+34%).
"Reduce booking time to 20 seconds" — achieved.
"Launch admin analytics" — achieved.
"Redesign UI" — achieved.
"Increase NPS to 40" — failed (37).
"Implement SSO" — achieved.
"Increase revenue by 25%" — failed (+4%).

Eight out of nine were about output or intermediate metrics. Only one was about revenue, and it had no owner: "owned by the product organization as a whole".
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Bookings indeed grew by 34%. Breakdown: growth came entirely from clients who were already active; the number of companies where more than half of employees use the product remained unchanged.

Corporate client churn: 11% → 16% over the year.

Churned client interviews show a repeating theme: "admins don't understand who occupies meeting rooms and how, so they have to resolve it manually."

Admin analytics was launched, but only 6% of admins use it: it was built as an on-demand export report.

Only 9% of client employees installed the mobile app.

Average check has not changed for two years; there was no price increase.

New client acquisition grew by 12% year-over-year—but churn ate up the gains.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Goals were gathered bottom-up: each team proposed their own, and the product director consolidated them into a list.

Nobody verified the connection between goals and revenue.

Bonuses were tied to the share of completed team goals.

Midway through the year, the team responsible for bookings found it easier to lift the metric by encouraging frequent short bookings; that is what they did.

There is no annual strategy; there is a 22-slide presentation on "development directions" with zero trade-offs.

There is no vision. To the question "why do we exist," the product director answers "we make convenient booking."

In addition to the main product, the portfolio includes two others: an access control system (growing market, small share, expected to generate revenue like the core product) and an old desktop client (small share, market moved on, unmaintained for two years).
fields.evidenceCards/3/title: What is proposed for next year
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Product Director: "Let's assign a revenue goal to every team."

One team: "We need our own goals; we don't directly affect revenue."

CFO asks for a churn goal.

Commercial Director proposes raising prices: no price hikes in two years.

One team suggests continuing work on the mobile app: "We've only just started."

The board expects 30% revenue growth next year.

Time to prepare: three weeks.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Tie goals to outcomes and clarify product roles
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Show why achieving goals failed to generate revenue, set one top-level goal with driver metrics beneath it, give teams metrics they can directly influence, and address the product portfolio.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
The analysis takes a week and clarifies the picture: eight out of nine goals were about output, while the only revenue goal had no owner. The 34% booking growth turned out to come from already active clients—and was partially gamed via short bookings because bonuses depended on the raw count.
The main gap is in churn: 11% → 16%, and lost clients report that admins don't understand who occupies rooms. Analytics was formally launched, but only 6% use it.
You set one top-level goal—churn below 10%—and driver metrics under it: share of companies where over half of employees use the service, and share of admins using analytics weekly. Each team gets a metric it directly impacts.
You differentiate the portfolio: access control gets bet status with validation metrics instead of revenue targets; desktop client gets sunsetted.
Price increases are handled as a standalone calculated decision, not a team goal.
Over the year, churn drops to 9.4%, and revenue grows by 27%.
Trade-off: some teams viewed shared metrics as a loss of autonomy, discussing it at every meeting for the first two quarters.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Set a revenue goal for every team
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: The product director is right: if everyone had a revenue goal, nobody would waste time on fluff. Assign each team a share of the revenue plan.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
Formally, goals become financial, which looks convincing in slides.
However, the platform/reliability team genuinely does not drive revenue: its goal becomes a fiction, ignored by mid-year.
Two teams argue over revenue attribution, bargaining instead of building.
Churn remains unowned because no team has a churn goal.
By year-end, revenue grows by 9%.
Trade-off: one extreme replaced another; setting a metric a team cannot influence works no better than setting a metric detached from money.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Set a single churn goal for everyone
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: The CFO is right: churn ate up all the gains. Make it the company's sole target for the year.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
The focus is right: 11% → 16% churn is indeed what killed growth, and targeting it shifts the discussion.
Teams look into churned clients and discover the same issue from the survey: admins don't know who occupies meeting rooms.
However, without driver metrics beneath it, five teams interpret the goal differently, and two feel they cannot influence it at all.
The product portfolio remains unmanaged: access control is still forced to generate core product revenue and stalls.
Churn drops to 12.5%—progress, but less than achieved otherwise.
Trade-off: the right primary metric, but lacking breakdown into actionable team drivers.
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Prices haven't been raised in two years, as suggested by the commercial director. This is the fastest way to hit revenue targets.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The math favors a price hike: two years without indexation on fixed pricing meant a slight increase would yield noticeable revenue.
However, the hike lands in a year when churn has already climbed from 11% to 16%, with the root cause unaddressed.
Some clients treat the price hike as the final reason to leave: churn hits 19%.
Revenue grows by 6% instead of the expected 20%.
Trade-off: right lever applied at the wrong time—prices should be raised where customers see clear value, not when they are already planning to exit.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Goal is defined as output rather than outcome, satisfied merely by releasing a feature
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Strategy fails to state where we choose not to play and what we explicitly abandon
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Uniform targets are applied across all products in the portfolio regardless of life cycle
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Vision fails to rule out any good ideas, making it ineffective
